chapter.name: Understanding Markets
chapter.blurb: What a market is, how prices are agreed, types of markets, wholesale and retail supply chains, the role of markets, the government's role and judging quality.

concepts.name: What is a market? The Hampi Bazaar
concepts.description: The meaning of a market, needs and wants, features of a market and the Hampi Bazaar of Vijayanagara.
concepts.idea: A market is a place where people buy and sell goods, and it needs a buyer, a seller and a price.
concepts.rule: A place where people buy and sell goods is a market, also called bazaar, haat or marukatte. It may be physical or online. Markets connect people, traditions and ideas. A need is what a person requires to survive, such as food and shelter; a want is something desired but not essential. Every market has a buyer and a seller who agree on a price. The Hampi Bazaar in the Vijayanagara Empire, opposite the Virupaksha temple, was praised by the Portuguese traveller Domingos Paes as the best-provided city in the world, with grains, oil, silk, animals, jewels and precious stones.
concepts.example: Hampi Bazaar sold grains, seeds, milk, oil, silk and animals such as horses and birds.

concepts.name: Prices and how buyers and sellers agree
concepts.description: Negotiation, demand and supply, and how prices settle at a level acceptable to both.
concepts.idea: Prices settle through interaction of buyers and sellers, each looking at what is acceptable.
concepts.rule: Buyers and sellers often negotiate and bargain to reach an acceptable price. If the seller fixes the price too high buyers may not buy; if too low the seller loses. With guavas, a seller at Rs 80 per kg and buyers asking for less negotiate until a mutually agreeable price such as Rs 40 is reached. Over time the amount offered by sellers and needed by buyers helps determine a price that is high enough for the seller and low enough for the buyer. Supply is the quantity sellers are willing and able to sell at a price; demand is the quantity consumers are willing and able to buy.
concepts.example: Vegetables are cheaper late at night at weekly markets, and woollen clothes are discounted at the end of winter.

concepts.name: Types of markets: physical, online, domestic and international
concepts.description: Physical and online markets, domestic and international markets, imports and exports.
concepts.idea: Markets can be physical or online and domestic or international.
concepts.rule: A physical market is where buyers meet sellers in person, such as weekly markets, haats, local markets and malls. Online markets use apps or websites so buyers and sellers need not meet; goods are delivered to the doorstep and services such as online classes are also available. Some services like tailoring need in-person contact. The share or stock market does not trade goods and services. A domestic market is within a country's boundaries; international markets cross borders through exports (selling abroad) and imports (buying from abroad). India was the world's largest importer of vegetable oils in 2024.
concepts.example: Palm oil is mainly imported from Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

concepts.name: Wholesale and retail markets and the supply chain
concepts.description: Producers, wholesalers, distributors, retailers, aggregators and the Surat textile market.
concepts.idea: Goods reach consumers through a chain of producers, wholesalers, distributors and retailers.
concepts.rule: Wholesalers buy goods in large quantities from producers or manufacturers, store them in godowns (with cold storage for perishables) and supply mandis or wholesale markets. Retailers buy from wholesalers and sell in smaller quantities to final consumers for consumption, not resale. Distributors bridge the gap between wholesalers and retailers over distances and difficult terrain. In online markets aggregators, websites or apps, combine offers from many sellers, hold bulk stock in warehouses and deliver to buyers. Surat, Asia's oldest textile market, receives raw cotton from cotton mandis and passes fabric through weaving and dyeing to wholesalers. Surat also has the world's largest diamond industry with about 1.5 million artisans.
concepts.example: Khari Baoli in Old Delhi is a famous wholesale spice market.

concepts.name: The role of markets in people's lives
concepts.description: How markets help access goods, signal what consumers want, employ women in Ima Keithal and carry traditions.
concepts.idea: Markets give access to goods, guide production and build relationships and culture.
concepts.rule: Markets facilitate transactions between producers and consumers and help people access goods they cannot produce. Without markets farmers could not sell and cloth makers could not buy cotton. Some products, such as art, have few buyers and sellers. Consumer demand guides producers: when many ask for refrigerators that use less electricity, producers make energy-efficient ones. Relationships develop between buyers and sellers across generations, such as with a tailor or the local grocer with a monthly account. Ima Keithal, the Mother's Market in Imphal, is run by about 3000 women, gives employment and is a melting pot of cultures. In south India sellers give free haldi and kumkum as a mark of goodwill.
concepts.example: Ima Keithal in Manipur is owned and run entirely by women.

concepts.name: The government's role in markets
concepts.description: Price controls, quality and safety standards, external effects, weights and measures and public goods.
concepts.idea: The government controls prices, ensures quality, reduces harmful effects and provides public goods.
concepts.rule: The government monitors interaction between consumers and producers. It sets maximum prices for essential goods such as lifesaving drugs and minimum prices for wheat, paddy and maize so farmers do not incur losses, and sets minimum wages. Prices must be set carefully: too low and producers stop producing; too high and consumers suffer. It sets quality and safety standards and tests medicines. It regulates external effects such as pollution from single-use plastics and checks weights and measures. Kautilya's Arthashastra told ghee sellers to give one-fiftieth extra as manasrava. The government also provides public goods such as parks, roads and policing, which producers do not expect to profit from.
concepts.example: The government sets a minimum price for wheat, paddy and maize.

concepts.name: Assessing quality: certification marks and reviews
concepts.description: How consumers judge quality using labels, FSSAI, ISI, AGMARK, BEE Star, reputation and online reviews.
concepts.idea: Certification marks and reviews help consumers judge quality and safety.
concepts.rule: A packet label shows net quantity, date of manufacture, best before date, MRP, name and address of the manufacturer, nutrition facts, batch number, allergen declaration, FSSAI mark and licence number and an ingredients list. FSSAI means Food Safety and Standards Authority of India and shows the food is tested and safe. The ISI mark, issued by the Bureau of Indian Standards, appears on electrical appliances, construction materials, tyres and paper. AGMARK certifies agricultural products such as vegetables, fruits, cereals, pulses, spices and honey. BEE Star ratings on TVs, laptops and air conditioners show energy efficiency; more stars mean less electricity. Word of mouth and online reviews also influence buyers.
concepts.example: More stars on a BEE label mean the appliance uses less electricity.
